The Impact of Hydrogels and Fertilizer on 
Radish Growth in Martian Regolith 
 
Radicle Roots 
 
Plant Mars Challenge: Fall 2025 
Undergraduate/Professional Division 
Team #23644 
 
Florida Institute of Technology 
Melbourne, FL 
 
Team Members: 
Amelia Thompson, Alex Leonard, Naomi Tomy, and Meada Watt 
 
Coach: 
Shane Doyle

Introduction 
In 1880, novelist Percy Greg wrote in his book “Across the Zodiac” about a space 
traveler who carried plants with him on his voyage to Mars, for the process of waste recycling 
(Eliot, 1986). 50 years later, the Russian scientist Konstantin Tsiolkovsky took this idea beyond 
mere science fiction and hypothesized that humans could, in fact, co-exist with plants under 
closed conditions on Mars (Wheeler, 2010). Future Martian missions require sustainable life-
support systems. An ideal life-support strategy for astronauts would be the one that utilizes in-
situ resources like soil, water, nutrients, and sunlight, which are available on Mars, to eliminate 
the need for constant replenishment and to minimize the transportation costs (Kasiviswanathan et 
al., 2022). Martian soil has a low water retention capacity (Peyrusson, 2021). Mars has water 
deposited in its equatorial regions, during the periods of high orbital obliquity, when the water at 
the poles became unstable and was contained at the equatorial regions (Wilson, et al., 2018). Yet, 
this water is not available for in-situ utilization. The physio-chemical characterization of the 
Martian regolith simulant MGS-1 has established the alkaline nature of Martian regolith 
(Caporale et al., 2024), with a pH above 6 due to the high concentrations of calcium perchlorate 
(Gilrain et al., 1999). Additionally, Martian regolith lacks the vital micronutrients, 
macronutrients and organic matter, which are the essential components for the proper growth and 
yield of plants (Nadeem et al., 2018). This deficit, along with the low water retention and 
alkalinity of the soil creates a hostile environment for the growth of plants. 
This study investigated the strategy of using hydrogels to retain water for plants on 
Martian regolith. Hydrogels are polymers that are able to absorb large volumes of water and 
retain it on the roots of the plants (Peyrusson, 2021). Likewise, by increasing the water 
availability, they allow the plants to reduce water stress and enhance plant growth even in the

harsh environment of Mars (Montesano et al., 2015). Moreover, bone meal was utilized as the 
fertilizer for our study, as bone meal is known for its slow-release of minerals like calcium 
(Hodson et al., 2001) and phosphorus (Bøen et al., 2013), which aids in cell elongation 
(Burstrom, 1968) and seed development (Malhotra et al., 2018). This study was done on Cherry-
Belle radishes Raphanus sativus L., a small-sized red radish. It is a root vegetable crop found 
worldwide and widely used in salads. It is packed with fiber, antioxidants, vitamin C, phenolic 
compounds and glucosinolates and can be used to reduce oxidative stress and to treat stomach 
disorders experienced in microgravity by the astronauts (Kim et al., 2016). 
This study tested the optimum condition for radish growth, by varying the Martian 
regolith simulant (MGS-1):potting soil ratios, and the concentration of fertilizers and hydrogels. 
We hypothesized that the radishes grown on the 50-50 fraction of MGS-1 simulant and potting 
soil, will show the greatest growth in terms of stem height, leaf length, radish length and 
diameter. 
 
Measurements and Methods 
The pots were set up in a large grow tent that contained an LED grow light array and a 
ventilation system to maintain constant growing conditions. There were 12 pots, organized into 
three groups of 4, based on the addition to the soil-regolith mixture. Specifically, the pots with 
hydrogels and fertilizer were grouped, the pots with just fertilizer were grouped separately, and 
the pots with no additives were grouped separately. The pots within each group were 
individually labeled with the percent composition of the regolith and the added material. Each 
group was placed on a bucket lid to reduce water leakage and soil spillage to other groups. All 
groups were placed along the right side of the grow tent, while another Plant Mars group had

their experiment on the left side, with about a foot of space between the two experiments. A 
visual representation of the growth setup (Figure 1). 
 
 
Figure 1 - Experimental Growth Setup. Each row varied in soil composition, and each column 
varied in the type of soil inclusions. 
 
The seeds were geminated in a humid environment for 1 week. They were then planted about 
half an inch deep and two seeds per pot with about an inch of space between them. Because of 
lack of growth and excessive mold in the pots with additives at around week 2, we replanted 
those in the same way, except we germinated for only 2 days instead. 
 
The radishes were watered every Tuesday and Friday with deionized water, and measurements 
were taken on Thursdays. If there was no one available to take measurements on Thursday, 
measurements for that week would be made on either Tuesday or Friday. All plants were given 
100 ml of water when first planted, then the amount was reduced to 50 ml after the first week.

The pots with hydrogels were reduced to 40 ml of water after we observed that they were being 
overwatered. The radishes received 12 hours of light every day, from 7:00 am to 7:00 pm; after 
the time change due to daylight savings, they received light from 6:00 am to 6:00 pm. The 
temperature of the grow tent was also monitored and kept between 20 and 25 degrees Celsius. 
All data was recorded on a shared Google Spreadsheet. 
The pH of the soil of each pot was measured using pH strips every week. The strips 
would be buried about a quarter of the way into moist soil or regolith and left to sit for about a 
minute. If the soil was not sufficiently wet to take measurements, the plant would be given water 
and left to drain for a few minutes before retesting the pH. Then, we would remove the strip and 
record the data in the spreadsheet. 
While the radishes were growing, we measured their stem height using a measuring tape 
and recorded the results in the spreadsheet. The stem was measured in centimeters from the soil 
to the base of the tallest leaf. If two radishes were growing in the same pot, their heights would 
be separated by a comma. At the end of grow week 8, the radishes were carefully uprooted, and 
the root length was measured, along with the length and diameter of any radish vegetable 
produced. These measurements were also done with a measuring tape in centimeters. 
There were several constraints to the experiment, including the time frame, the amount of 
regolith supplied, and the presence of mold. During the time frame of eight weeks, only three 
small radishes were produced. The small harvest size was limited by the need to restart some of 
the pots due to excessive mold. After the first week, mold began growing on the group that had 
fertilizer and the group that had fertilizer and hydrogels. We decided to replant those with the 
regolith we had left. Mold continued to grow in the new pots; however, we were able to mitigate 
and stop its growth by spraying them with a 3% hydrogen peroxide solution.

Results and Analysis 
Over the eight-week growth period, we found that the radishes grown with no soil 
inclusions demonstrated the largest stem length root growth, radish diameter, and radish length . 
Pots with fertilizer and hydrogels showed some root growth, but did not yield harvestable 
radishes. These observations did not align with our original hypothesis, which stated that 
radishes grown in pots with 50% Martian regolith and 50% potting soil would yield the largest 
diameter. Measured stem length, root length, radish diameter, and radish length are presented in 
the tables below.

Discussions and conclusion 
 
Before planting the radishes into the pots they were germinated, during the first germination the 
seeds were left to germinate too long and mold was created. The moldy seeds and the seeds with 
little to no mold were picked apart and the ones with no mold were put into the pots. Each pot 
got two seeds with an inch between them. After two weeks of watering, these plants were filled

with mold, particularly the soil composition with hydrogels, in all probability because hydrogels 
store moisture. The mold was addressed with hydrogen peroxide spray (3%), and seemed to get 
rid of the mold well. After about four weeks, the pots with no sign of plant growth were 
replanted. 
 
The pH of the no inclusion 100% potting mix stayed in the 7.0s, the pH of the no inclusion 50% 
regolith had 7.0s but a few 8.0s, and the pH of the no inclusion 75% regolith stayed in the 8.0s 
fully (Table 5). These pH results can lead to the conclusion that martian regolith is basic 
compared to regular potting soil that is neutral. This means that changing the pH of the martian 
regolith to be more neutral may be a major contributor to plant growth in mars regolith. 
 
 In total, eight plants had sprouted leaves and grown. Only three of those plants yielded radishes 
to be harvested. The three soil compositions being: No inclusion 100% potting soil, no inclusion 
50% regolith and 50% potting soil, and no inclusion 75% regolith and 20% potting soil (Table 
4). The 100% potting soil yields the largest radish with a length of 3.0cm and diameter of 2.5cm 
(Table 3 and 4). The results of the experiment lead to the conclusion that no inclusion of 
hydrogels or fertilizer and 100% potting soil will lead to the best results of radish growth. The 
hydrogels would break up the soil when they grew after being watered, which may have stunted 
the radish growth. Fertilizer did more harm than help the radishes grow in the regolith. However, 
when looking at the other two radishes grown in 50% potting soil/ 50% regolith and 75% 
regolith/ 25% potting soil, it seems that even with no inclusions the radishes still grew. This can 
lead to the conclusion that radishes would be a good choice as a plant to grow in mars regolith 
because it has shown endearment in the regolith even in the absence of inclusions.
